With a new aluminum case, the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition feels like a high-end piece of tech. With a thinner body and square edges, this new Kindle feels more like a smartphone or tablet than it does an e-reader.

With adjustable warmth and brightness, you can read with it in bright summer sun at the beach and then turn it down and warm it up when you're in a dim bedroom. And speaking of the beach, its IPX8 rating makes it safe to use in the bath or at the pool.

Plus, the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition comes in more exciting color options. While the Paperwhite just comes in graphite, the Signature Edition also comes in a stunning seaglass green.

Don't get us wrong, though; we still love the Kindle Paperwhite. If you want to save $50, the next best e-reader you can buy is the basic Kindle Paperwhite. It's still a quick, well-rounded e-reader but doesn't come in fun colors and has lockscreen ads.

It has an IPX8 rating, so you don't need to fear if it slips into the bath. I wish it had page-turn buttons, but you could also use it with the Kobo Remote if you want to avoid touching the screen.

Having tried my hand at more than a dozen e-readers in all shapes, sizes, and brands, I wasn't expecting to be so deeply impressed by the Kobo Clara Colour, but it is a wonderful e-reader. With a 6-inch screen, it's slightly smaller than the Kindle Paperwhite, but its size allows you to hold it comfortably for multiple hours at a time without any wrist or arm fatigue.

In my previous testing with Kobo devices, I've really liked them, but one sticking point is that they're slower than Kindles. Initially, I found that the Kobo Clara kept up with the Paperwhite, but after several months of use, it had a tendency to lag. Compared to Kindles, I had to manually sync the Kobo Clara to get my library books to show up.

Its processing system is otherwise really smart and fixes one of my biggest e-reader pet peeves. When you adjust the font size on a Kindle, the device doesn't recalculate how many pages are in the book, making it inaccurate, so you don't know exactly how many pages you have left in a chapter. The Kobo Clara does recalculate page count accurately for a more exact reading experience. Though, one thing to note: Kobo counts the number of digital pages, whereas Kindle page numbers typically match up with physical book copies.

For a lower price than the Kindle Paperwhite, the Kobo Clara offers color displays, something you can't get in the Kindle lineup unless you're willing to spend $290. The colors aren't as bright as you'd experience in a physical book, but they're still vivid enough to enjoy a graphic novel.

Its Libby (aka Overdrive) integration is seamless, and e-books you borrow on your library card will automatically populate on your account. You can browse and borrow library books directly from the e-reader, instead of having to whip out your phone app. However, for users who use Libby to the max with multiple library cards, be warned: you can only log in to one account at a time.

The Kobo Clara's biggest downfall is its battery life. It's supposed to last up to 42 days, although many online users say it averages out at about two weeks. That's quite pathetic in the face of the Kindle's 12-week battery life; however, I'd trade in a better reading experience over a couple weeks of battery life any day.

No, not all e-readers are waterproof. All of the e-readers in this guide are waterproof, with an IPX8 rating. That means the device can be fully submerged in two meters of water without harm to the device.

But if you're looking at e-readers like the basic Kindle or e-readers from Boox, be cautious before using them near water, as none of these e-readers have waterproof ratings.

Yes, with their IPX8 rating, these e-readers can be fully submerged in water. However, there's a limit to the water exposure. The devices can only be submerged up to two meters for up to 60 minutes.

So if your e-reader falls into the bath, pick it up as soon as possible, dry it off, and shake off as much water as possible.

All of these e-readers are tested using the same criteria as every e-reader we test. In addition to analyzing the devices' performance and value, we prioritized waterproof rating and special features.

In this guide, we only included e-readers with waterproof ratings, knowing that if you're reading in the bath, it will definitely be exposed to water. The devices had to have an IPX8 rating, which makes them safe to be submerged in water.

We prioritized e-readers with page-turn buttons, a rare feature on e-readers. This allows you to turn the page without touching the screen with wet fingers. Since so few devices have page-turn buttons, we also chose e-readers that could be used with page-turn covers or remotes.

Tech is expensive these days, so we also considered value. If a device was over $200, it had to have special features that made us prioritize it over a more affordable device. We included devices at a variety of price points so no matter your budget, you can find a waterproof e-reader.

#635. A radical theory says the universe is twice as old as we thought

A radical alternative to the standard picture of the cosmos is gaining attention after researchers at the University of Ottawa reported that it successfully matched several important astronomical observations. The model suggests that the Universe could be 26.7 billion years old, nearly twice the widely accepted age of 13.8 billion years, and that neither dark matter nor dark energy is needed to explain its behavior.

If further research supports these findings, the theory could offer a very different explanation for how the Universe evolved. It may also help resolve one of modern astronomy's most puzzling discoveries: the existence of surprisingly large and mature galaxies at a time when the conventional model suggests they should barely have begun forming.

Throughout 2025 and 2026, Rajendra Gupta, an adjunct professor in the University of Ottawa's Department of Physics, and postdoctoral researcher Dr. Nikolaos Samaras evaluated an alternative cosmological framework known as CCC+TL against several major astronomical observations.

The name stands for “covarying coupling constants plus tired light.” Rather than relying on dark matter and dark energy, the model proposes that some of the effects attributed to these mysterious components could result from changes over time in fundamental physical constants. These constants help determine how particles and forces interact.

For decades, astronomers have searched for direct evidence of dark matter and dark energy. Dark matter is thought to provide additional gravity that helps explain how galaxies move and how large cosmic structures hold together. Dark energy is the name given to whatever is causing the expansion of the Universe to accelerate. Although extensive observations support their gravitational and cosmological effects, neither component has been directly identified.

The prevailing cosmological framework, called ΛCDM, incorporates both. Despite its success in explaining a wide range of observations, it faces questions raised by the discovery of unexpectedly developed galaxies in the early Universe.

“Most emerging models explain only a limited set of observations,” Professor Gupta says. “A new model must not conflict with the pillars of cosmology and astrophysics, and our findings meet that challenge, including the yet-to-be-published Cosmic Microwave Background challenge.”

Testing such a fundamentally different theory requires more than adjusting the standard model. CCC+TL modifies the Einstein and Friedmann equations, which describe gravity and how the Universe expands. As a result, Gupta and Samaras had to develop equations and computer programs specifically adapted to their model for each test.

The researchers report that CCC+TL produced results consistent with several major astronomical measurements. One important test involved the light elements created shortly after the Big Bang, including hydrogen and helium. The alternative model predicted abundances that matched those calculated using the standard cosmological framework.

It also agreed with cosmic chronometer measurements, which allow astronomers to reconstruct the history of cosmic expansion by comparing the ages of galaxies at different distances. These measurements provide an independent way to examine how the expansion rate has changed over billions of years.

Another significant test focused on the motion of galaxies. In a recent study published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, the researchers examined all 175 galaxies in the SPARC database. They found that their model could reproduce the observed rotation curves without invoking dark matter.

Rotation curves describe how quickly stars and gas orbit at different distances from the centers of galaxies. Under conventional gravity, the visible matter alone generally cannot explain these motions, which is one of the major reasons scientists believe dark matter exists.

The team also investigated time dilation in observations of supernovae. Time dilation refers to the apparent stretching of events over time when viewed across vast cosmic distances. Their analysis offered additional support for CCC+TL, although the research paper remains under review.

The researchers also examined the Bullet Cluster, a famous system of colliding galaxy clusters that provides some of the strongest observational evidence for dark matter.

In this system, most of the ordinary matter is concentrated in extremely hot gas that emits X-rays. However, observations show that much of the gravitational effect is associated with the galaxies rather than the gas. The standard explanation is that invisible dark matter passed through the collision along with the galaxies.

Under CCC+TL, the additional gravitational effect predicted by the model also follows the galaxies instead of the hot gas, but without requiring dark matter. The researchers emphasize that this result is only an initial proof of concept and that more detailed investigations are necessary.

“Observations attributed to dark matter and dark energy likely originate from covarying coupling constants,” adds Professor Gupta, who examines this possibility further in a separate paper exploring the origin of dark matter and dark energy.

Perhaps the most intriguing implication of the model involves the earliest galaxies ever observed.

Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have discovered galaxies that appear surprisingly massive and mature for their early place in cosmic history. Their existence has prompted questions about how quickly stars and galaxies could have formed after the Big Bang.

CCC+TL offers a possible answer by giving the early Universe substantially more time to develop.

In the standard cosmological model, the Universe was approximately 300 million years old during the period known as cosmic dawn, when the first generations of stars and galaxies were emerging. At the same observed redshift, however, CCC+TL would place the Universe's age at roughly 4.6 billion years.

Redshift measures how much light from a distant object has shifted toward longer, redder wavelengths. Astronomers use it to study distant galaxies and investigate earlier stages of cosmic history.

Under the alternative model, galaxies observed at extremely high redshifts would have had billions of additional years to grow. The researchers calculate that early galaxies would be approximately 12 times larger in both size and mass than predicted by standard cosmology, according to findings published in Galaxies 13, 115.

“Impossible early galaxies become predictable galaxies,” Professor Gupta explains. “We predict that galaxies exist well beyond the distances the James Webb Space Telescope has reached.”

Upcoming observations could provide an important opportunity to investigate this prediction.

The James Webb Space Telescope's GLIMPSE program aims to search for extremely distant galaxies, potentially reaching redshifts greater than 50. These observations would probe an exceptionally early period in the Universe's history under the standard cosmological framework.

According to conventional models, there may not have been enough time for large galaxies to assemble at such extreme redshifts. The CCC+TL model does not impose the same restriction because its cosmic timeline allows substantially more time for galaxies to develop.

Finding galaxies at these distances could therefore provide another important way to compare the competing explanations. However, such discoveries would not, by themselves, establish that the alternative model is correct.

Although the researchers report encouraging results across several major cosmological tests, CCC+TL remains an unconventional proposal that requires further independent examination. The standard cosmological model continues to explain a broad range of astronomical observations, and any replacement must ultimately demonstrate comparable or greater success.

For Gupta, the latest findings provide a reason to continue investigating the possibility that the Universe operates differently than scientists currently assume.

“The success should encourage astronomers to take the new model seriously. It is challenging to understand and apply, but we believe it extends the physics of the Universe beyond ΛCDM limits,” concludes Professor Gupta.

#631. After 40 years, CERN finds evidence of a one-in-10-billion particle decay

After more than 40 years of searching, physicists at CERN have reached a major milestone in their hunt for one of the rarest known particle decays. Researchers working with the LHCb experiment have detected evidence of a process expected to occur only once in approximately 10 billion beauty particle decays.

The finding, announced during a seminar at CERN, marks the first time a single experiment has produced sufficient evidence for this extraordinarily rare event. Beyond its rarity, the decay is particularly valuable because it could help scientists investigate particles that are too massive to be created directly in the Large Hadron Collider.

At the center of the discovery is a particle called Bd, which contains a beauty quark and a down antiquark. Scientists found evidence that this particle can decay into a pair of muons (μ+μ-). Muons are similar to electrons but have greater mass. The results agree with predictions from the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions, and help narrow the possibilities for new particles beyond it.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal New Physics

One reason physicists are so interested in these unusual decays is that quantum effects allow other particles to influence how they occur. Even particles too heavy to be produced in the Large Hadron Collider can potentially leave subtle traces in the rates of these processes.

By measuring extremely rare decays with high precision, researchers can look for differences between experimental results and theoretical predictions. Such discrepancies could provide indirect evidence of previously unknown particles. Generally, the rarer a decay is, the more sensitive it can be to these hidden influences.

The decay known as Bd → μ+μ-belongs to a special category that physicists have long considered 'golden channels' for investigating physics beyond the Standard Model. During this process, a beauty quark and an antiquark with the opposite electric charge annihilate each other. Their energy is transformed into a muon and its antiparticle.

Scientists have previously observed a related process involving a different beauty particle, called Bs. In 2015, a joint analysis by the LHCb and CMS collaborations reported the first confirmed observation of Bs → μ+μ-, along with initial evidence for the much rarer Bd decay.

However, subsequent analyses incorporating data collected through 2018 could not confirm the earlier evidence for Bd → μ+μ-. The difference in rarity is substantial. The Bs decay occurs approximately three times per billion beauty particle decays, while the Bd process is predicted to happen about 30 times less frequently.

Upgraded CERN Detector Makes the Breakthrough Possible

A significant improvement to the LHCb experiment helped researchers overcome the enormous difficulty of detecting such a rare event.

Following a major upgrade, the experiment began collecting data in 2024 at five times the rate achieved between 2010 and 2018. The upgraded detector also became better at identifying different kinds of particles, giving researchers a clearer picture of the activity produced during collisions.

The team combined these improvements with machine learning techniques to distinguish the exceptionally rare signals from the vast number of other particle processes. Without these advances, the events scientists wanted to study would have been overwhelmed by the background.

"Physicists have been chasing this decay for more than forty years," said Marco Santimaria, who co-led the international analysis team of 19 scientists. "Extreme precision is required to pick the muons out of the overwhelming background."

Four Decades of Searching Finally Produce Strong Evidence

In particle physics, scientists use a statistical measure called standard deviations to evaluate how likely an apparent signal is to result from random fluctuations rather than a genuine physical process.

A result must reach three standard deviations to qualify as evidence of a new phenomenon. At that level, the probability of random fluctuations producing a signal at least as statistically extreme is approximately 0.3%.

Using data collected during 2024 and 2025, the LHCb researchers identified evidence of Bd → μ+μ- at a significance of 3.0 standard deviations. When they combined those measurements with earlier data gathered between 2011 and 2018, the statistical significance increased to 3.2 standard deviations, exceeding the widely accepted threshold for evidence.

The same investigation also produced the most precise measurements ever obtained for the related Bs → μ+μ-decay, providing additional information about these exceptionally uncommon processes.

Although the new findings represent a major achievement, physicists have not yet reached the threshold required to declare a confirmed observation. That milestone requires a significance of five standard deviations.

If future measurements achieve that level of certainty, Bd → μ+μ-would become the rarest beauty particle decay ever observed.

Future Large Hadron Collider Upgrades Could Uncover Hidden Particles

Researchers expect upcoming improvements to the Large Hadron Collider to make these measurements even more powerful.

The High Luminosity LHC, also known as the HiLumi LHC, is scheduled to begin operating in 2030. Another major upgrade to the LHCb experiment is planned for the middle of the following decade. Together, these developments could eventually increase the experiment's data collection rate by another factor of ten.

Collecting much larger datasets would allow physicists to detect more of these extremely rare decays and measure their properties with greater precision. That increased sensitivity could make it possible to identify subtle effects associated with particles that remain beyond the direct reach of existing accelerators.

"Seeing evidence of this rare decay is incredibly exciting, opening up new possibilities to probe beyond the direct reach of the LHC," explained Harry Cliff, LHCb's Rare Decays Convener and Analysis Co-lead.

"The future LHCb upgrade will allow us to observe many more of these decays, providing even greater sensitivity to undiscovered particles."

For physicists who have pursued this elusive signal for more than four decades, the new evidence represents a long-awaited advance. It also offers a promising way to investigate whether the known laws of particle physics are part of a much larger picture.

#630. Moderna raises 2026 outlook as CEO says newer vaccines are gaining traction

Moderna on Friday smashed third-quarter revenue and earnings estimates and hiked its outlook for full-year sales growth, as some of its newer products gain momentum and Covid vaccine revenue outperforms.

Shares of Moderna rose roughly 3% in premarket trading on Friday.

The biotech company now expects 2026 revenue growth of 15% to 25%, up from its previous guidance of up to 10%.

"The new product and the diversification of geography is what has led to such a strong Q3," Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said in an interview ahead of the results.

For example, he said the company is seeing the "full-year impact" of its next-generation mRNA Covid vaccine, which won U.S. approval in May 2025. Bancel noted that Covid is a seasonal business and vaccine contracts are typically established in the first quarter, so Moderna's shot only had a "small launch" to start with last year.

Moderna's new stand-alone flu shot, which was approved in the U.S. in August, will similarly have a "limited launch" in the country in 2026 given the timing, he said.

In a separate interview on CNBC's "Squawk Box," Bancel said Moderna's geographic expansion in Canada, the U.K. and Asia helped boost results. The company's work to lower costs also resulted in a profit in the quarter, he added.

"It's the sales that are stronger and the costs that are also lower," Bancel said.

Here's what Moderna reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Moderna's third-quarter revenue jumped 29% to $1.31 billion, boosted by higher Covid vaccine sales in international markets and helped by deliveries under long-term government partnerships. Revenue was $780 million in the U.S. and $533 million in international markets.

The company posted a net income of $162 million, or 38 cents per share, for the third quarter. That compares with a net loss of $200 million, or a loss of 51 cents per share, reported for the year-ago period.

The results come weeks after Moderna and Merck unveiled promising late-stage data on their experimental personalized cancer vaccine in combination with immunotherapy Keytruda in certain melanoma patients. Despite the positive results, investors battered Moderna's stock after part of the data was leaked on social media just days before trial investigators were set to present it at a European medical conference.

Bancel called it a "surprising reaction," but said that the companies also saw a positive response from others on Wall Street, including long-term investors and analysts who examined the full data in depth. He added that the doctors in the field "were so impressed with the data," and many expressed that they hope to use it in their day-to-day practice.

Moderna's stock has skyrocketed more than 700% this year, largely on optimism about the potential for the shot.

#628. NASA reveals bold new plan to return astronauts to the Moon in 2028

NASA has revealed new details about its accelerated effort to return American astronauts to the Moon in 2028. The updated strategy includes testing two competing lunar landers, streamlining rocket preparations, and introducing a lighter spacesuit to help make the first moonwalks possible sooner.

During an October 23 briefing, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other agency leaders outlined the next steps for the Artemis program. The revised approach centers on two major missions: Artemis III, a test flight scheduled for 2027, and Artemis IV, which is intended to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.

The announcement builds on priorities introduced earlier this year through NASA's Ignition initiative. Agency officials also highlighted recent progress in spacecraft development, mission preparations, and partnerships with private aerospace companies. These efforts are intended to reduce technical risks, accelerate the schedule, and establish the foundation for a lasting American presence on the Moon.

"This is a very energized NASA, and these updates are only a small part of that story. We are bringing extreme focus to the mission to ensure delivery of world-changing outcomes as quickly, safely, affordably, and successfully as possible," said Isaacman. "NASA is driving outcomes to make Moon missions a reality, and we're not waiting for others to bring their plans to us -- the campaign must move with urgency as strategic competitors pursue a permanent presence beyond Earth."

Artemis III Will Test Two Lunar Landers in Earth Orbit

Before attempting another crewed Moon landing, NASA plans to conduct a major rehearsal in Earth orbit. The Artemis III mission will bring together NASA's Orion spacecraft and experimental lunar landers developed by SpaceX and Blue Origin.

Four astronauts will travel aboard Orion, launching on NASA's powerful SLS (Space Launch System) rocket. During the planned 14-day mission, the crew will practice rendezvous and docking procedures with both companies' lander test vehicles. Rendezvous involves guiding two spacecraft to meet in orbit, while docking allows them to connect so astronauts can move between vehicles.

These demonstrations are designed to verify important spacecraft capabilities before Artemis IV attempts to carry astronauts to the Moon's surface.

The tests will take place in a carefully planned sequence. Blue Origin will first launch a test version of its Blue Moon lander into Earth orbit. NASA will then send Orion and its four astronauts into space aboard the SLS rocket, where Orion will rendezvous and dock with the Blue Moon vehicle.

Next, SpaceX will launch a test version of its Version 3 Starship lunar lander. Orion will separate from Blue Moon and perform another docking maneuver, this time with Starship. By testing both systems during a single crewed mission, NASA aims to gather essential operational experience while reducing uncertainties before the 2028 landing attempt.

NASA Cuts Rocket Preparation Times and Costs

The new mission details follow other recent Artemis progress reports. According to NASA, the hardware needed for Artemis III remains on schedule, and improvements in processing have reduced preparation timelines by approximately 50%.

The agency also reported a significant engineering achievement involving a critical rocket fuel-line component. Rather than relying on an outside supplier, NASA engineers redesigned, manufactured, and tested the component themselves in just five months. The work cost roughly one-tenth of an earlier estimate from an external vendor.

"NASA should be expected to do this kind of work, and we have some of the best technical knowledge in the world on rocket hardware and operations to do it," said Jeremy Parsons, the agency's Artemis program manager. "It's an example of how we are rebuilding our core competencies and developing centers of excellence in technical functions instead of continuing to outsource expertise."

The improvements reflect NASA's broader effort to strengthen its internal engineering capabilities, shorten development schedules, and reduce the cost of preparing missions for launch.

SpaceX and Blue Origin Offer Different Paths to the Moon

For Artemis IV in 2028, NASA intends to launch astronauts aboard Orion using the SLS rocket from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Once in space, the crew will rely on a lunar landing system developed by either SpaceX or Blue Origin to reach the Moon's surface.

Both companies have revised their original mission designs to make operations simpler, more efficient, and more adaptable. Although they share the same objective, their approaches to transporting astronauts to the lunar surface differ considerably.

SpaceX plans to use its Starship spacecraft, which will take on additional propellant while orbiting Earth. After refueling, Starship will meet Orion and carry the spacecraft toward the Moon. Refueling in orbit is an important part of SpaceX's strategy because it allows the vehicle to receive the propellant needed for its journey after leaving the launchpad.

Blue Origin is developing a different approach using its Blue Moon Mark 2 lander. Its plan calls for additional propulsion stages in Earth orbit to send the lander toward the Moon. The lander will then meet Orion in a relatively low lunar orbit before carrying astronauts down to the surface.

Both companies are working toward having their systems ready to support a crewed Moon landing in 2028. Maintaining two potential landing systems gives NASA greater flexibility as development and testing continue.

NASA Explores New Rocket Options for Artemis IV

NASA is also considering two possible upper stages for the SLS rocket used on Artemis IV. An upper stage is the portion of a rocket that provides additional propulsion after the earlier stages have completed their work, helping send a spacecraft toward its destination.

One option is the interim cryogenic propulsion stage already used by SLS. The other is an extended version of United Launch Alliance's Centaur V upper stage, which would hold additional propellant.

By developing both possibilities, NASA hopes to preserve flexibility in its launch plans and avoid becoming dependent on a single technical solution. Having alternatives could help the agency respond to engineering challenges without jeopardizing the broader Moon landing schedule.

A New Lightweight Spacesuit Could Speed Up Moonwalks

Another important change involves the spacesuits astronauts will wear while exploring the lunar surface.

NASA is working with Axiom Space on a second, lighter design known as the "Sortie suit." The new suit is intended specifically for the first Moon surface excursions and weighs approximately half as much as Axiom's larger primary spacesuit.

The lighter design could simplify preparations for the earliest landing missions and help astronauts begin exploring the lunar surface sooner.

However, the Sortie suit is not intended to replace the primary design. Axiom's more capable suit will remain part of NASA's plans for future missions that require longer periods outside the spacecraft and more demanding surface activities.

Building a Permanent Human Presence on the Moon

NASA's ambitions extend well beyond returning astronauts to the lunar surface for a single mission.

As the Artemis program advances, the agency intends to send crews on increasingly challenging expeditions near the Moon's South Pole. This region is an important focus of future lunar exploration, and the missions are designed to expand how much of the Moon humans can investigate directly.

NASA describes the effort as part of a new Golden Age of innovation and exploration. The agency expects its lunar missions to support scientific discoveries, generate economic benefits, and encourage the development of technologies needed for more ambitious space exploration.

Ultimately, the goal is to establish an enduring human presence on the Moon rather than repeat the brief visits of earlier lunar expeditions. The experience gained from operating spacecraft, supporting astronauts, and carrying out increasingly complex missions on the lunar surface will also help NASA prepare for another historic objective: sending the first astronauts to Mars.

#625. Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee

A first taste of black coffee can be surprisingly unpleasant. Its sharp bitterness is the kind of flavor our brains are naturally inclined to avoid. Yet millions of people eventually come to enjoy that same taste, often looking forward to their morning cup. What changes?

Scientists at UC San Francisco may have uncovered an important part of the answer. Their research reveals a little-understood dopamine pathway linking the digestive system and the brain, helping explain how we develop a liking for certain flavors through repeated experience.

Dopamine is a chemical messenger involved in motivation, reward, and learning. Researchers have long known that it helps the brain recognize experiences worth repeating. However, most studies have examined rapid dopamine signals that appear within seconds of encountering something rewarding, such as the sight of a favorite meal.

The new research, published November 4 in Nature, examines a different system. This slower pathway responds to information coming from inside the body, allowing the brain to learn about the benefits of food after it has been consumed.

"We've shown that this slow dopamine system is what drives us to learn to like certain foods over time, and we can see where and how that happens," said Zachary Knight, PhD, professor of Physiology and senior author of the study.

The findings offer a possible explanation for why an initially unpleasant flavor can gradually become enjoyable. Once the brain connects the taste of coffee with caffeine's stimulating effects, Knight explained, "that coffee starts to taste a lot better."

How the Gut Sends Reward Signals to the Brain

Scientists have spent decades investigating dopamine and its influence on behavior. Its familiar, rapidly acting signals help us respond to opportunities for reward. But dopamine also operates on a slower timescale, through a system that has received far less attention.

According to Knight, this slower process largely unfolds outside our conscious awareness.

When food enters the digestive tract, specialized sensors detect nutrients, including sugar and fat. Information about those nutrients travels toward the brain, where it can produce a dopamine response that develops gradually and continues for several minutes.

To investigate this process, Knight worked with James Grove, PhD, who was a graduate student at the time. They introduced nutrients directly into the stomachs of mice while monitoring dopamine activity throughout their brains.

The researchers used either sugar water or a liquid resembling a milkshake. Delivering these substances directly into the stomach allowed them to separate the effects of nutrients from the experience of tasting food.

The results revealed a powerful, prolonged dopamine response in a specific brain region called the anterior basolateral amygdala, or BLA.

The amygdala is involved in emotional processing and learning, including forming associations between experiences and their consequences. Scientists already knew that dopamine was released in this particular region, but its purpose had remained unclear.

"We could see that this dopamine is part of a different system and begin to understand its role," he said.

Scientists Find a Brain Circuit That Changes Food Preferences

Finding the dopamine signal was only the beginning. The researchers next wanted to determine whether it actually influenced how animals learned to prefer different flavors.

They first interrupted the newly identified pathway in mice. The animals continued eating normally, indicating that the disruption did not prevent them from consuming food. However, they lost the ability to learn that an unfamiliar flavor was associated with receiving calories.

The team then conducted the opposite experiment.

After mice tasted a flavor containing no calories, the researchers artificially activated dopamine fibers in the BLA. Remarkably, the animals developed a preference for that flavor even though it provided no nutritional reward.

In effect, stimulating the pathway reproduced the learning signal that nutrients would ordinarily generate.

Together, the experiments showed that this dopamine system plays a critical role in teaching the brain which flavors predict rewarding nutritional effects.

A Surprising Discovery in the Left Side of the Brain

The researchers also looked for evidence that a comparable process occurs in humans. Brain imaging studies conducted by Knight's collaborators revealed a strikingly similar pattern.

Dana Small, PhD, a psychologist at Yale University, revisited data from an earlier positron emission tomography (PET) study involving 13 men. Participants had consumed either a milkshake or a drink without calories.

Her analysis found that dopamine release following nutrient delivery was especially concentrated in the left side of the BLA.

A separate study led by Marc Tittgemeyer, PhD, and his colleagues provided additional evidence. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures changes in brain activity associated with blood flow, the researchers examined 38 adults after they consumed glucose, a simple sugar.

They observed increased activity in the same brain region.

One of the most unexpected findings was that the response was not evenly distributed between the brain's two hemispheres.

In both mice and humans, nutrients produced a considerably stronger dopamine response in the left BLA than in the corresponding region on the right.

That imbalance surprised Knight because brain networks responsible for essential functions, such as feeding, are generally expected to work in a relatively symmetrical fashion.

Why the left side plays such a prominent role remains unanswered. Knight's laboratory is now investigating what causes this unusual difference.

Could This Discovery Help Scientists Change Food Cravings?

Identifying the pathway provides researchers with a clearer picture of how the digestive system influences the brain's learned responses to food. It also raises an intriguing possibility: Could scientists eventually use this knowledge to change which foods people find appealing?

One area of interest involves GLP-1 medications, a class of drugs that mimic a hormone naturally released by the gut. These medications can substantially alter appetite and eating behavior.

Knight's team did not investigate GLP-1 drugs in the new study, so it remains unknown whether they influence the dopamine pathway the researchers identified.

Still, Knight suggests that one possible explanation for some of their effects could involve reducing the dopamine signals generated when nutrients reach the digestive system. If that happens, foods might gradually become less rewarding because the brain would receive weaker signals reinforcing their flavors.

For now, this remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated effect of the medications.

The broader implications extend beyond hunger and fullness. Many approaches to changing eating behavior focus on reducing appetite or increasing feelings of satisfaction after a meal. The newly mapped pathway suggests that the brain's process of learning food preferences could eventually become another target.

By influencing how the brain connects flavors with their consequences, future treatments might someday help people develop different preferences rather than simply making them feel less hungry.

"By understanding the steps between nutrient detection in the gut and learning in the brain, it might be possible to fine-tune them to subtly change our preferences for different foods," Knight said.

The discovery offers a new perspective on why our tastes can change over time. From learning to enjoy bitter coffee to developing a preference for calorie-rich foods, what we love to eat may depend partly on a quiet conversation between the gut and brain that continues long after the first bite.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants R01-DK106399, R01-DK138127, R01-NS116626, and R01-DK145100 and F31-NS120468).

#623. Scientists discover that necks didn't evolve for the reason we thought

The first animals to make the transition from water to land nearly 380 million years ago may have had a surprising limitation: they could barely turn their heads. Although scientists have long believed that the evolution of necks gave these pioneering creatures greater freedom to look around, new research suggests their necks were actually remarkably stiff.

The discovery challenges a decades-old explanation for why animals developed distinct necks in the first place. Rather than evolving to improve head movement, necks may have emerged as part of broader changes to the skeleton that allowed animals to use their front limbs for movement.

To investigate this possibility, an international team of researchers combined new fossil evidence with experiments on living fish and computer models of ancient anatomy. Their findings, published October 14 in the journal Nature, offer a new perspective on one of the most important evolutionary transitions in Earth's history.

"This is a really interesting time in Earth's history where some of the first forests are forming, and there's a really radical reorganization of the Earth," said Tom Stewart, an assistant professor of biology at Penn State and a member of the research team. "So, understanding exactly when our lineage made that transition from water to land, how it was achieved, and which anatomical systems were changing is an important part of that story. What's cool is that many of the changes that were occurring in the skeleton at this time, about 380 million years ago, are still reflected in our own bodies today."

Why Scientists Thought Animals Evolved Necks

For decades, the prevailing explanation was that necks evolved to give early tetrapods, the ancestors of four-limbed vertebrates, greater control over their heads as they adapted to life outside the water.

The reasoning seemed straightforward. An animal living in shallow water or moving onto land would benefit from looking downward or turning its head from side to side to locate prey, recognize threats, and explore its surroundings. A flexible neck would allow it to do this without repositioning its entire body.

Modern fish generally lack a distinct neck because their shoulder structures connect directly to their skulls. To look in another direction, they typically have to turn their bodies instead. Separating the head from the shoulders therefore appeared to be an important step toward greater mobility.

However, determining how these ancient animals actually moved has been difficult. Much of their backbone consisted of soft tissue that rarely survives long enough to become fossilized, leaving scientists with an incomplete picture of how their necks functioned.

"The fish that were undergoing these changes had a vertebral column that was largely made up of soft tissue, which, unlike bone, is rarely preserved in the fossil record," Stewart said. "In these cases, we can look to modern animals to serve as analogues for the past, like how living birds can teach us about now extinct dinosaurs."

Ancient Fish Fossils Reveal a Turning Point in Evolution

Some of the best evidence for the transition from water to land comes from fish that lived during the Devonian Period, approximately 420 to 360 million years ago.

These ancient animals possessed an unusual combination of features. While they retained many characteristics of aquatic fish, some had stronger, more substantial fins that may have helped support their weight. Such adaptations could have allowed them to lift themselves off the bottom or push through shallow water.

At the same time, certain species began showing a clear separation between the skull and shoulders, creating the first distinct necks.

One especially important example is Tiktaalik, a fossil fish first described in 2006. Its remains were discovered on Ellesmere Island in Nunavut, Canada, in the northern Arctic. Because Tiktaalik is closely related to the earliest vertebrates with limbs, its anatomy provides valuable clues about the evolutionary changes that eventually made life on land possible.

"Tiktaalik is one of these fossil fish, and it was first described in 2006," Stewart said. "It has been reasonably assumed for decades that this separation of head and shoulders must have allowed the head to move more freely, so the hypothesis that neck mobility was an evolutionary driver for this change in the tetrapod body plan has prevailed, at least until now."

Tiktaalik also helps researchers understand other major changes that occurred during this evolutionary transition, including the shift from drawing food into the mouth through suction underwater to biting on land, as well as the gradual transformation of swimming structures into limbs used for walking.

"The materials have been really important because Tiktaalik is one of the closest relatives to limbed vertebrates," Stewart said. "It helps us to reconstruct a lot of intermediary steps in the transition to life on land, such as the move from suction feeding in water to biting on land or from swimming to walking."

How Modern Sturgeon Helped Solve an Ancient Mystery

The key to testing the traditional explanation for neck evolution came from an unexpected source: the sturgeon, a modern fish sometimes described as a living fossil because it retains several ancient anatomical features.

Early tetrapods had backbones that were very different from those of most vertebrates living today. Instead of relying primarily on a series of large vertebrae connected by joints, their spinal columns contained a prominent structure called the notochord.

The notochord is a long, flexible rod of tissue that runs through the vertebral column and helps support the body. In these ancient animals, the individual vertebrae were relatively small and arranged around a much larger tube of soft tissue.

Because this arrangement responds to forces differently from a modern backbone, researchers had struggled to determine how much flexibility it would have allowed. That uncertainty prevented them from directly testing the idea that necks initially evolved to improve head movement.

Sturgeon provided an opportunity to overcome that problem. Although they are only distantly related to the ancient animals being studied, their backbones have a similar notochord structure.

The research team measured the stiffness and mechanical properties of the notochord in modern sturgeon. They then incorporated those measurements into models of fossil animals, including early tetrapods such as Tiktaalik, to estimate how far their necks could actually move.

The results were striking. Even when the head and shoulders were anatomically separated, the structure of the backbone would have severely restricted movement. The earliest necks appear to have been much less flexible than researchers had assumed.

"We know that tetrapods did eventually gain higher neck mobility," said Dana Korneisel, a postdoctoral researcher at Uppsala University in Sweden and first author of the paper. "Clearly it was advantageous eventually, but it was not an advantage available to these early tetrapods yet because of the limitations of their anatomy."

The researchers had expected the new models to clarify how much additional movement early necks provided. Instead, they found that most of the animals they examined would have gained little ability to reposition their heads.

"I undertook this study to find out how big of a difference this change in anatomy made for these animals," Korneisel said. "The vertebral columns of sturgeon are built a lot like those of early tetrapods, but they didn't seem terribly stiff. So, after doing the modeling, the lack of significant head mobility for almost all of these animals was a huge surprise."

The findings suggest that the first animals with distinct necks could not simply turn their heads to survey their surroundings the way many modern land animals can.

Their ability to lift their heads was also extremely limited, sometimes falling below what would be expected in fish.

"Head elevation in these animals was no more than what you would expect in fish and, sometimes, even less," Korneisel said. "We found that the kind of head twisting that we can do when we shake our heads was not feasible in any of these animals."

The researchers also cautioned that their estimates may actually overstate how much movement was possible.

Their models considered the mechanical properties of the backbone itself, but other structures would have added further restrictions. Muscles, skin, and even bones embedded within the skin of some early tetrapods may have made their necks still more rigid.

Necks May Have Evolved for Walking Before Looking

Together, the findings point to a different explanation for the origin of the neck.

Instead of first appearing because animals needed to turn their heads, the separation of the skull and shoulders may have developed alongside anatomical changes that allowed the front limbs to support and move the body.

In other words, the earliest necks may have been a consequence of adaptations for locomotion rather than an adaptation for improved vision or head movement.

Greater neck flexibility eventually evolved and became an important advantage for land vertebrates. But the new evidence suggests that this benefit came later, after the basic structure of the neck was already established.

The discovery also highlights the importance of the notochord in understanding animal evolution. Backbones dominated by this structure are uncommon among living vertebrates, but they were widespread during much of Earth's history. Studying modern animals that retain similar anatomy can therefore help scientists reconstruct how extinct creatures moved and behaved.

"We want to understand how these early tetrapods were living and how that is reflected in changes to their bodies," Stewart said. "Trying to reconstruct where an animal lived, how it moved, what its behavior was, is a really difficult thing. The cool part of this story is that it combines data from fossils and studies of living animals in a mechanical, functional perspective to reconstruct what the changes we see in the animal's anatomy mean for their behavior."

By bringing together fossil discoveries, experiments on living fish, and biomechanical modeling, the researchers have challenged a familiar explanation for an anatomical feature that remains central to the bodies of humans and many other vertebrates today.

Along with Stewart and Korneisel, the international research team included Cassandra M. Donatelli of the University of Washington; Linfang Han, Marcos Martinez, Tetsuto Miyashita, and Emily M. Standen of the University of Ottawa in Canada; and Andrew L. Traynor, Benjamin K. A. Otoo, and Hillary C. Maddin of Carleton University in Canada.

The research received support from The Steven Cohen Award for Student Research, presented by the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology, and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (RGPIN-06442). The authors are solely responsible for the content, which does not necessarily reflect the views of the funding organizations.

#620. Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but new research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.

Scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord. The findings could help explain why some people with Alzheimer's experience changes in walking, balance, or coordination long before noticeable memory problems emerge.

The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook important problems elsewhere in the body.

The research was led by James Hickman, a professor at UCF's Nanoscience Technology Center, and Research Professor Xiufang "Nadine" Guo, working alongside scientists at the healthcare technology company Hesperos. Funded by the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging, the study used laboratory systems built from human cells to investigate how inherited Alzheimer's mutations affect movement. The findings were published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association.

"Motor deficits may be an earlier indication [of Alzheimer's]," Guo says. "If we can detect those changes and intervene earlier, that could help delay the onset of central nervous system symptoms."

Why Alzheimer's Symptoms May Appear Before Memory Loss

Alzheimer's is generally associated with progressive memory loss, confusion, and declining cognitive abilities. However, doctors have also observed that some patients develop physical symptoms, including changes in balance, coordination, and gait (manner of walking), years before clear cognitive difficulties become apparent.

These observations have raised an important question: Are such movement problems simply a consequence of damage occurring in the brain, or could Alzheimer's also interfere directly with nerves elsewhere in the body?

To investigate, the UCF team focused on familial Alzheimer's, a rare inherited form of the disease that typically develops earlier in life (from 40 to 65 years of age) than the more common form.

Their experiments revealed that motor neurons carrying mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's could disrupt the connections responsible for controlling muscles, even when the brain and spinal cord were completely absent from the experimental system.

Motor neurons are specialized nerve cells that transmit signals to muscles, telling them when to contract and produce movement. The new findings suggest that Alzheimer's mutations can interfere with this process directly, rather than affecting movement only through damage to the brain.

"This is the first time it's been demonstrated that deficits in the peripheral nervous system can arise directly from these mutations," Hickman says. "It means drugs that target the brain may not fix problems in the rest of the body."

The peripheral nervous system includes the nerves located outside the brain and spinal cord. These nerves carry signals between the central nervous system and the rest of the body, helping control movement, sensation, and other essential functions.

Guo also points out that preserving the ability to move could have benefits beyond physical health. Regular physical activity is associated with better cognitive well-being, so protecting motor function may also help support brain health.

How a Miniature Human Cell System Revealed the Discovery

To examine the relationship between Alzheimer's mutations and muscle movement, the scientists used an innovative laboratory platform known as "human-on-a-chip" technology.

Developed and manufactured through Hesperos, a company co-founded by Hickman, these miniature systems bring different types of human cells together under controlled conditions. They allow researchers to recreate specific biological functions and observe how diseases interfere with them.

Unlike conventional laboratory experiments that examine isolated cells, these systems can reproduce important interactions between different tissues. They also provide an alternative to animal models, which do not always accurately reflect how human diseases behave.

For this study, the team created a miniature model of the neuromuscular junction, the connection where a motor neuron communicates with a muscle cell.

The model was deliberately designed without a brain or spinal cord. This was a crucial part of the experiment because it allowed the researchers to investigate whether Alzheimer's-related changes could cause movement problems independently of the central nervous system.

The scientists combined healthy muscle cells with motor neurons derived from stem cells that carried genetic mutations associated with familial Alzheimer's disease. Stem cells are cells that can develop into specialized types of cells, making them valuable tools for studying human diseases in the laboratory.

The researchers then examined how effectively the altered nerve cells communicated with otherwise healthy muscle tissue.

The results showed that the Alzheimer's-associated mutations could interfere with normal nerve-to-muscle function. This suggests that at least some movement difficulties linked to the disease may arise directly in the peripheral nervous system rather than being caused entirely by degeneration in the brain.

Why Damaged Nerve Connections Can Affect Walking and Balance

Every voluntary movement depends on successful communication between the nervous system and the muscles.

At the neuromuscular junction, an electrical signal traveling along a motor neuron triggers chemical communication that causes a muscle to contract. This process makes everyday activities possible, from walking and maintaining posture to lifting objects and performing precise movements.

When the connection becomes impaired, muscles may respond less effectively to nerve signals. Depending on the severity and location of the problem, this can contribute to weakness, reduced coordination, and difficulty sustaining physical activity.

To evaluate these effects, the research team measured how consistently nerve signals produced muscle contractions and how long the muscles could continue contracting before becoming fatigued.

These measurements provided a direct assessment of how well the nerve and muscle cells worked together. They also resemble aspects of the functional testing physicians use when examining patients with movement disorders.

"You can't move unless the motor circuit works," Hickman says. "When a doctor taps your knee to check your reflex, they're testing that exact connection."

By demonstrating impaired nerve-to-muscle communication in a system containing no brain or spinal cord, the study provides evidence that mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's can produce effects beyond the central nervous system.

However, the experiments do not establish that these changes necessarily occur before memory loss in patients. Further research will be needed to determine how closely the laboratory findings reflect the progression of Alzheimer's in people, particularly those with the more common forms of the disease.

Could This Discovery Lead to Earlier Alzheimer's Detection?

The findings suggest a potentially important new direction for Alzheimer's research: looking beyond memory and other cognitive symptoms when investigating the disease.

If future studies confirm that changes in motor function are detectable early in certain patients, tests of walking, coordination, or nerve-to-muscle activity might eventually help identify disease-related changes before more obvious neurological symptoms develop.

The results also raise questions about treatment. Many Alzheimer's therapies are designed to address processes occurring in the brain, but medications that target the central nervous system may not necessarily correct abnormalities affecting peripheral nerves and muscles.

Understanding these separate effects could help researchers investigate treatments that protect physical function alongside cognitive health.

Human-on-a-Chip Technology Could Transform Disease Research

Beyond the implications for Alzheimer's, the researchers see considerable potential in using human-on-a-chip systems to investigate other diseases and evaluate possible treatments.

Because these platforms contain human cells and reproduce measurable biological activities, they can help scientists observe disease-related changes in conditions that more closely resemble human physiology than some conventional experimental models.

This approach may be particularly useful in drug development, where researchers need to understand not only how a potential treatment affects individual cells but also how it influences interactions between different tissues.

Such systems can also uncover biological effects that may be difficult to detect in animal experiments, potentially helping researchers identify promising therapies and recognize limitations earlier in development.

For Hickman, the progress represents the culmination of three decades of work devoted to understanding disease through more realistic laboratory models.

"These systems let us study disease in a way that's closer to what actually happens in the human body, and that's what we need to develop better treatments," he says.

#617. Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin

A badly distorted British silver coin dating to 1834 may hold evidence of an unusual accident during the minting process nearly 200 years ago. New scientific analysis suggests that the remarkable damage to the coin was more likely caused by a manufacturing problem than by ordinary wear, corrosion, or a later impact.

The findings, reported by IA STUDIO in the journal npj Heritage Science, center on a silver sixpence issued during the reign of King William IV. The coin was found in an album containing various coins at a car boot sale in Greater Manchester, England. Although the sixpence had an individual price tag of £8, the entire album was subsequently purchased as a single lot rather than the coin being bought separately.

What makes this particular sixpence remarkable is the extent and unusual pattern of its damage. Its central surface appears severely crushed and distorted, yet much of the outer rim and the small grooves along its edge remain relatively intact. The contrast raised an intriguing question about what could have happened to the coin.

To investigate, researchers examined the silver piece using powerful microscopes, chemical testing, and detailed three-dimensional surface measurements. The results point toward an unusual sequence of intense compression, potentially while the coin was being struck at the mint.

A Crushed Silver Coin Reveals Unusual Clues

The most striking evidence came from the coin's severely distorted central regions. Detailed measurements revealed deep, sharply defined depressions, elevated ridges, stepped surfaces, and areas where the metal appeared to have been pushed and displaced in overlapping patterns.

These features were particularly pronounced on the front of the coin, known as the obverse, which bears the portrait of William IV. Across the damaged central portrait area, the difference between the highest and lowest measured points reached approximately 0.75 millimeters.

That may sound small, but it represents a substantial distortion on the surface of a thin silver coin.

The investigators found that the overall damage was most consistent with repeated applications of high pressure concentrated in a limited area. The metal also appears to have been at least partly prevented from spreading outward as the force was applied.

This combination of heavy central damage and relatively well-preserved edges is difficult to reconcile with the gradual effects of circulation or simple corrosion. It also makes a single later impact, with the metal free to move outward, a less convincing explanation.

Instead, the findings favor an unusual problem during the original striking process, although the available evidence does not establish the exact sequence of events with certainty.

Microscopic Analysis Reveals Damage Beneath the Surface

To better understand the unusual deformation, the investigation combined scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDX) and optical surface profilometry.

The microscopic and chemical examinations provided information about the coin's metal composition and the changes affecting its surface.

In areas that had escaped the worst damage, testing identified an underlying silver and copper alloy. The more severely distorted regions contained lower measured concentrations of silver, higher levels of copper, and additional chemical evidence associated with corrosion and contamination.

These substances were especially concentrated inside the depressions formed by the damaged metal.

However, the chemical results largely reflected changes at the surface. Although corrosion and contamination had affected the coin, they could not adequately account for the depth, shape, and distribution of its unusual distortions.

The team also used optical surface profilometry, a technique that maps the height and shape of a surface in three dimensions. This made it possible to examine the coin's damaged areas in much greater detail than ordinary photographs could provide.

The resulting maps showed steep depressions, raised shoulders, abrupt changes in surface height, and multiple layers of metal displacement.

Using height measurements supplied by the Oxford Materials Characterisation Service, the study's author determined that the damaged central portrait region varied in height by approximately 750 micrometers, equivalent to 0.75 millimeters.

Taken together, the findings suggest that the coin underwent repeated compression while its sideways movement was at least partly restricted. This explanation fits the evidence better than ordinary wear, which generally smooths a coin's surface over time, or corrosion, which tends to remove or chemically alter material.

A Rare Glimpse Into 19th-Century Coin Production

The sixpence was produced in 1834, when Britain was already using steam-powered presses to manufacture coins.

During this period, coins with serious striking defects were typically identified through mint inspections and melted down so the metal could be reused. This was especially important for coins made from precious metals such as silver.

If the unusual deformation occurred during the original minting process, the sixpence may therefore represent a rare surviving example of a manufacturing failure that would ordinarily have been removed from circulation before it ever reached the public.

Such a coin could provide a physical record of a brief mechanical problem during the early era of mechanized coin production.

Determining whether the damage actually occurred at the mint is challenging, however. Historic metal objects can undergo many changes over decades or centuries, and severe deformation may obscure the physical clues needed to identify its origin.

To address this uncertainty, the study examined several kinds of evidence independently. The researchers considered the composition of the underlying metal, chemical changes at the surface, and the three-dimensional geometry of the deformation before comparing the results with different possible explanations.

The findings also demonstrate how non-destructive scientific techniques can be used to investigate other historic metal objects. By combining chemical and structural evidence, researchers may be able to distinguish manufacturing defects from later damage even when visual inspection alone provides no clear answer.

How AI Helped Investigate the Coin Mystery

The investigation also explored how computational tools, including artificial intelligence, could assist in evaluating a historical mystery without replacing physical scientific evidence.

Before any laboratory results were available, the author began by studying high-resolution photographs of the sixpence and systematically reviewing its unusual surface features.

This early examination helped identify several possible causes of the damage and establish what kinds of physical measurements would be needed to test them.

Human-supervised computational tools, including large language models (LLMs), helped organize the observations, develop alternative explanations, compare competing ideas, and formulate questions that could later be investigated through laboratory testing.

Importantly, the initial hypotheses and analytical notes were recorded before the independently produced laboratory measurements became available.

The possible explanations included ordinary circulation wear and corrosion, mechanical damage occurring after minting, later compression under restricted conditions, and deformation during the original manufacturing process.

To investigate these possibilities, independent measurements were commissioned from the Experimental Techniques Centre at Brunel University of London and the Oxford Materials Characterisation Service within the Department of Materials at the University of Oxford.

Once the testing was completed, computational tools were used again to help organize the resulting data and compare the physical findings with the earlier explanations.

"The important sequence was hypothesis first, independent laboratory measurement second," said A. Ikraam, founder of IA STUDIO and author of the study.

"We used the models to ask what features mattered and what evidence could distinguish one explanation from another. Then the laboratory measurements gave us something physical to test those ideas against. The models could support the reasoning process, but they could not decide what happened to the coin."

Scientific Evidence Points to a Possible Minting Error

Although artificial intelligence played a supporting role in organizing observations and evaluating competing possibilities, it did not produce the laboratory measurements or determine the final findings.

The study's conclusions were based on independently generated scientific data, with the author retaining responsibility for interpreting the evidence and deciding which explanation was best supported.

The results favor a rare minting anomaly involving repeated, highly concentrated pressure, rather than damage caused by ordinary circulation, corrosion, or a single unrestricted impact after production. Nevertheless, the research does not conclusively establish every detail of what happened to the sixpence.

Beyond shedding light on the possible origins of a strangely mangled 1834 coin, the investigation illustrates how modern imaging, chemical analysis, and carefully evaluated computational tools can work together to uncover clues hidden in historic objects.

What initially appeared to be little more than a badly damaged silver coin may instead preserve an unusual record of how something went wrong during the early days of mechanized coin manufacturing.

#615. Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production in Texas next year to ramp Cybercab, Musk says

Tesla CEO Elon Musk on Friday said the electric vehicle maker will "be winding down" production of the Cybertruck at its Texas gigafactory around the middle of next year.

Musk, who hailed the Cybertruck as the future of the pickup truck segment, said in a post on X early Friday morning that the end of production at the massive facility would make room for manufacturing of its Cybercab robotaxi.

The Cybertruck is exclusively produced at the company's plant in Texas alongside the Tesla Model Y and two-seat Cybercab, which Musk has touted as a crucial product for the automaker moving forward.

Musk did not say whether the company would produce the Cybertruck at a different facility, but he later responded to a user on X who called the update an "end of an era" and said the Cybertruck was the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made."

"True, but the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time," Musk said.

Tesla began Cybertruck deliveries in late 2023. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC.

The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales, despite Musk's pre-launch prediction that annual sales would eventually total 250,000.

"Trucks have been the same for a very long time," Musk said when the truck was unveiled in 2019. "Like 100 years. Trucks have been basically the same. We want to try something different."

While Tesla does not break out its sales by model or region, Cox Automotive estimated sales of the Cybertruck last year at 20,237 units in the U.S., down 48% from 38,965 in 2024.

One big buyer of the Cybertruck last year was Musk's aerospace and tech conglomerate, SpaceX, which spent $131 million buying up the angular steel trucks at Tesla's suggested retail price, according to a SpaceX financial filing.

The distinct look of the vehicle made some owners a target of rude gestures and more serious road rage, one owner told CNBC last May, after Musk became the biggest funder of Donald Trump's presidential campaign and led the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, an effort to slash the federal workforce and regulations.

Wired wrote in an October 2025 feature story, "There is likely no object that feels more emblematic of US president Donald Trump's return to the White House than the Tesla Cybertruck." The magazine interviewed owners who described being spit on and sworn at due to their choice of vehicle.

The Cybertruck's specifications also fell short of those Tesla advertised early on, and in some cases fell short of those offered by leading fuel-burning pickups. There have also been many quality and production problems associated with the vehicles.

The 2024 Tesla Cybertruck was the subject of 11 voluntary recalls, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration website. Issues ranged from a "trapped" acceleration pedal risk that could cause unintended acceleration, to software defects and an inverter fault that could result in sudden loss of drive power.

#614. NASA’s CHAPEA Mars crew finally emerges after more than a year in isolation

After spending more than a year experiencing what life could be like on Mars, four NASA volunteers have finally stepped outside, marking the end of an ambitious experiment designed to prepare humans for future missions to the Red Planet.

The crew completed their simulated Mars journey on October 31, 2026, emerging into the outside world for the first time in more than a year. Although the volunteers never actually left Earth, their extended mission recreated many of the challenges astronauts could encounter while living and working millions of miles from home.

The experiment was part of NASA's Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) program, which investigates how people adapt to the demanding conditions of extended space exploration.

The four volunteers were Matthew Montgomery (left), James Spicer (middle left), Ross Elder (middle right), and Ellen Ellis (right). Following the completion of their mission, the crew posed together outdoors, celebrating their return from a simulated journey to another planet.

Throughout the experiment, the participants carried out tasks similar to those that future Mars explorers may need to perform. These included operating and testing essential systems, caring for crops, conserving limited supplies, and conducting extravehicular activities.

Extravehicular activities, often called spacewalks, are operations astronauts perform outside their spacecraft or habitat. In a Mars simulation, these activities help researchers examine how crews might prepare for and carry out work beyond the safety of their living quarters.

The volunteers also had to manage communication delays, an important challenge for anyone traveling to Mars. Unlike astronauts aboard the International Space Station, who can communicate with Earth almost instantly, future Mars explorers will experience significant delays because radio signals take time to cross the enormous distance between the two planets.

These delays mean astronauts cannot always depend on immediate guidance from mission control. They must be prepared to solve problems, make decisions, and manage unexpected situations with greater independence.

One of the biggest challenges of sending people to Mars is keeping them healthy, productive, and safe during long periods away from Earth. A crew must be able to manage food, equipment, living conditions, and daily responsibilities while working together in a confined environment.

NASA uses analog missions to explore these challenges before attempting actual journeys into deep space. An analog mission is a realistic simulation that reproduces selected conditions of space exploration while allowing scientists to study how people respond in a controlled setting on Earth.

The CHAPEA program provides an opportunity to investigate how astronauts might handle the practical demands of extended missions, including resource limitations, equipment maintenance, food production, and communication difficulties.

The lessons learned from Montgomery, Spicer, Elder, and Ellis will help NASA plan future human exploration missions. Their experiences are expected to inform the development of NASA's planned Moon Base and preparations for eventual crewed expeditions to Mars.

Although this crew's journey took place entirely on Earth, the knowledge gained could help address some of the challenges humans will face when they finally travel to the Red Planet.
